newsitem.title: PERU: FEATURE-Peru hostage saga to make heroes and villains.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Peru hostage saga to make heroes and villains.

text.p: Once the dust has settled around the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence, Peru's marathon hostage crisis could seal the fates and fortunes of many of its chief protagonists.

The future of the two main players -- President Alberto Fujimori and Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini -- hinges on the outcome of the siege now well into its third month. But politicians, diplomats and political experts who have followed the crisis closely say others already know what to expect.

They predict, for example, that senior heads in the security forces will roll for a perceived lapse that allowed a small band of young rebels to storm with apparent ease one of the most important diplomatic buildings in Lima.

On the other hand, the "stars" among the rebels' 72 VIP captives -- Japanese Ambassador Morihisa Aoki and Peruvian Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela -- are likely to receive a hero's reception if they come out safely. And chief Red Cross representative Michel Minnig, seen shuttling to and from the residence since the first days of the crisis on humanitarian and mediating missions, is already jokingly being touted as a candidate for the next presidential election in 2000.
Lower-profile figures such as government negotiator Domingo Palermo and the Vatican and Canadian government's mediators could also emerge as heroes if they pull off a peaceful solution.

"There's an awful lot at stake here -- most importantly 72 lives, but also a lot of people's reputations and future prospects," said a Latin American diplomat who was initially held hostage at the residence but later released.
FUJIMORI ANNOUNCES PROBE

Fujimori this week admitted for the first time his security forces had been at fault and announced an investigation into responsibility for the crisis. "We will have to take measures against those responsible," he said.
Opposition leaders have held their fire so far but will be gunning for resignations once the crisis is over.

"It's incredible that no one has resigned so far," one of the government's fiercest critics, legislator Javier Diez Canseco of the United Left party, told Reuters. "If you have someone incompetent why keep that person on?"

Opposition parties plan to target Armed Forces head Nicolas de Bari Hermoza Rios, leaders of the National Intelligence Service, Interior Minister Juan Briones Davila and National Police Chief Ketin Vidal. Other targets could ironically include the handful of other senior security and intelligence officials being held in the residence.

"I think that Hermoza and (top intelligence adviser Vladimiro) Montesinos will be protected, but Fujimori will probably sacrifice Vidal or Briones at a certain moment, not immediately," Diez Canseco said. "Intelligence has been pursuing the press and opposition instead of concentrating on the fight against these guerrilla, terrorist movements."

The roughly 15 MRTA rebels spent months meticulously planning their spectacular assault on the residence and took control of the building -- with more than 500 cocktail party guests inside -- within minutes.

A secret intelligence report obtained by Reuters showed that a regional anti-terrorist police unit warned headquarters in Lima weeks before the takeover that the MRTA was planning such an assault around Nov. 30. The unit said the MRTA had infiltrated heavily armed fighters into Lima to form an elite squad to carry out high-profile operations.

"Among the actions to be carried out would be the abduction of political and/or military personalities who would be used to pressure the government into releasing Tupac Amaru terrorist criminals in prison," it said.
FOREIGN MINISTER CHIEF BENEFICIARY

The chief political beneficiary of the crisis may be Foreign Minister Tudela, who has been praised by former hostages for his calm leadership inside the residence and his immediate willingness to help with cleaning chores.

"All Peruvians should be proud of their foreign minister," Dominican Republic Ambassador Jose Diaz said after his release. "He has shown an important attitude. Before going, I congratulated him. I felt comforted when I saw his courage."

But Tudela, 41, who was threatened with execution early in the crisis, could face friction with Fujimori when he comes out. The minister annoyed his boss with early implorings via walkie-talkie for the government to talk to the MRTA and consider an official peace negotiation with the group.

He was also reported as complaining to fellow hostages that the government had cut off secret telephone numbers to Fujimori that he tried to reach in the first hours of the crisis. The government later cut all phone contact to the residence, which also apparently angered Tudela.

"Tudela has become a popular figure. Without intending it, he has become a rival of the government," political analyst Pedro Planas said, predicting that Tudela would have to leave the government if he comes out unharmed.

"He was already a strong figure and now his political reputation is even higher and tinged with an atmosphere of heroism. I could see him as a strong presidential candidate in 2000," said a legislator from the government party who asked not to identified.

Tokyo's envoy Aoki, acutely embarrassed by the crisis that began while he was hosting a party, was expected to be replaced when he gets out but he has won deep affection from former hostages and the large Japanese community here.

An open letter from the hundreds of former captives recently praised his "gentlemanly, loyal and dedicated" conduct within the residence. That included sharing his clothes and other possessions among the hostages and a dignified appearance before the world's press in which he offered "a thousand apologies" for the crisis.
